newsitem.title: THAILAND: Securitisation seen partial help for Thai lenders.
newsitem.headline: Securitisation seen partial help for Thai lenders.

text.p: Loan securitisation offers a cheap funding alternative for distressed Thai lenders but is a limited solution to firms with the most seriously distressed portfolios, debt experts told a conference on Thursday.
Securitisation is a process in which firms sell the projected repayments on asset-backed loans or future revenues to a third party.
The third party then issues debt instruments backed by the repayments which removes the risk to investors from falling collateral values and exposure to the original lender.
Thai lenders, hard hit by a decline in the country's economic fundamentals and a slump in the property market, face a growing non-performing loan problem and urgently need alternative funding.

"Provided there is some cash flow transactions it is in theory possible to structure a securitisation but in practice it is by no means easy to do so," said Anthony Dixon, vice president of Salomon Brothers Inc.
"The execution of these transactions is somewhat difficult," he added. Applying the technique to very poor portfolios required exotic securitisation variations, he said.
Some estimates put non-performing loans in the finance sector sector as high as 31.5 percent.
Securitisation has helped alleviate distressed financial situations since it was first used to tackle problems in the United States housing market in the 1970s.

The process could help ease corporate liquidity in the finance and industrial sectors, executives. Liquidity has tightened since investor confidence has waned as the country's economic problems have intensified.

Legal restrictions have caused the few previous Thai securitisation-style issues to be structured so the the third party debt issuer has been designated as a leading secured creditor. Ownership of repayments by the third party has been restricted by law.
The Thai cabinet recently eased some legal restrictions on securitisation but more reforms were required to accelerate the process in Thailand, the conference was told.
"Thailand has clearly taken a major step with the new laws however there are still some issues which remain outstanding," Neil Campbell, senior associate at lawyers Freshfields said.

Value added tax, witholding tax restriction and the legal status complications currently made securitisation costs prohibitive and required further reform if the the process is gain in popularity, he said.
